judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: Plain, slightly stiff shop greetings with a jab at a rival inn and the class-as-title address ('sir [Group]'); unshowy in the way Nox's real vendors are.

items.label: B
items.critique: Each line is a tidy stock-fantasy quip ('best ale this side of the mountain', the price-gouging gag with 'Heh, heh'); every shop gets a joke, which is too even.

items.label: C
items.critique: The long, odd, insulting tirade with 'Hmmmph!' and repetition ('up and down, up and down'), the drawn-out 'Ahhhhhhhh...', and 'young sir' are pure Nox eccentricity.

items.label: D
items.critique: Dialect ('aye mate', 'Ya') plus a flat expository magic-shop line that just states who supplies whom; this unpolished informativeness is Westwood's.

items.label: E
items.critique: Every line has a crafted twist (impatient innkeep, coffins sold alongside arms, desperate mage); the 'coffins' gag reads as a borrowed motif and the set is too uniformly characterful.

items.label: F
items.critique: Built around the town's theme (fish, half drowned), slogan-like and cosy; fine game writing but tailored and generic rather than Nox's quirky plainness.

items.label: G
items.critique: The pushy 'Let's get to know each other! Buy something!' and the ominous mortician offering 'funerary services or ... goods' with ellipses and a page break are distinctive Nox.

items.label: H
items.critique: 'Beds upstairs, coffins out back' plus 'Heh, heh, heh' and 'finest steel under the mountain' are polished punchlines; it reworks the funeral-shop joke rather than having Nox's own oddness.

items.label: I
items.critique: The over-long official shop name 'outfitters to the Watch' feels like Westwood's formal signage; the grumpy inn line and 'jingle' gag are more modern, so this is a close call.

items.label: J
items.critique: Short, terse, formulaic lines ('This is [Person]'s', 'be quick about it') that echo the shapes of other texts (the Keep, 'don't see many') without a distinctive voice.

tells: Generated sets give every shopkeeper a neat one-line joke or personality hook; Westwood's sets are uneven, with one strange or rambling line beside flat, functional ones.
Generated lines lean on tidy stock phrases and slogans ('best ale this side of the mountain', 'finest steel under the mountain', 'fresh fish and a warm bed').
Recycled motifs across new texts (coffins at the inn or arms shop, 'Heh, heh') signal imitation of a single memorable Westwood line.
Westwood uses drawn-out interjections and odd spellings ('Hmmmph', 'Ahhhhhhhh...'), dialect ('aye mate', 'Ya'), and plain expository statements about factions, which the new texts rarely do.
New texts tailor greetings to the town's theme (fish, drowning, mountains); Westwood's vendors talk about the player, rivals, or their trade, not the setting's gimmick.
